en: The Mahāyāna Sūtra of the Crown King,
translated by Prince Yueposhouna of the Kingdom of Ujjayinī during the Liang Dynasty.
Homage to the Honored One of Perfectly Pure Awakening, the Ocean of Great Wisdom.
Thus have I heard:

At one time the Buddha was staying at the Āmra Grove in Vaiśālī together with a great assembly of eight hundred bhikṣus, ten thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and the various devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of supernatural beings, including ghosts and spirits.

At that time, when it was mealtime, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered the great city of Vaiśālī to beg for food; within that city, he proceeded in due order through the streets and alleys of the Quarter of Pure Fame.

At that time, in the streets and alleys of Viśuddhaghoṣā, there was a young boy named Sucintita. His nurse was holding him up in a high tower on a multi-storied pavilion; while playing and enjoying himself with a lotus flower in his hand, by virtue of his past roots of goodness, he spoke this verse to his nurse:
"Such sounds of music as these have never before existed in the world.
Mother, release me quickly now; I wish to go down from the pavilion."
This must be one of great diligence, the World-Honored One of Great Radiance;
I wish to cast my right foot toward the side of Indrakīla.
It is subtle and most delightful, with flocks of birds all gathered around it.
This sound has never been heard before, nor has it ever been seen arising;
it must be one of great diligence who, out of compassion for sentient beings,
has stepped with his right foot upon the side of Indrakīla.
Like a mother wearing a necklace, which she fastens to adorn her body;
though it has not yet been touched, it emits a wondrous sound that delights the mind.
This must be the Honored One among Gods, adorned with the radiance of merit.
He set down his right foot at the edge of Indrakīla;
like a man striking a bronze drum, a great sound issued forth,
and in every direction, this sound was heard by all.
This must surely be the Sun among Men, the Great Muni of radiant light,
who has entered this great city to benefit all sentient beings.
It is like when a tree bears flowers, adorned with every variety of blossom.
Uttering wondrous sounds at will, causing sentient beings to become attached—
this must surely be the Great Naga King, the Honored One who dwells well among the devas.
I wish to tread with my right foot upon the side of Indrakīla.
Like the sky, pure and stainless, pervasive and free from dust or obscuration,
with a radiance like the color of gold that causes the light of the sun to fade—
this must be the One Delightful to Behold, the Honored One endowed with perfect brilliance.
He set down his right foot at the edge of Indrakīla.
Thus these hosts of devas, dwelling in the air,
rejoiced and offered praise, circling about in the sky.
He who will surely benefit the world, the most supreme Honored One among the gods,
has descended by placing his right foot down beside Indrakīla.
Thus, all the sentient beings of this city have given rise to hearts of loving-kindness.
Each thought to themselves, as if mother and child were in close kinship:
"This must surely be a mass of merit, adorned with the flowers of virtue.
He then lowered his right foot and descended to the side of Indrakīla.
Just as a man or a woman, holding various exquisite flowers,
stands in attendance with hands full, gazing upon one another with joy—
surely such a person is a dragon among men, adorned with the flowers of merit.
He stepped down with his right foot upon the edge of Indrakīla.
Heavenly flowers and human flowers filled the void of space;
scattered in profusion as fragrant blossoms, they caused the hearts of men to rejoice.
"He must be one of great diligence, wishing to invite the Unsurpassed Honored One to enter the city of Vaiśālī for the benefit of all sentient beings.
At that time, having heard her son’s words, the wet nurse was struck with such terror that her hair stood on end; she immediately took the boy down from the upper story and thought to herself:
"To whom did those words belong? Who was it that spoke them?
Was it a deva? Or was it a nāga, yakṣa, rākṣasa, piśāca, kiṃnara, or mahoraga?"
"Is he for such a person?
He remained where he was, without moving.

At that time, when the World-Honored One arrived at his gate, the youth saw the Buddha, the World-Honored One, beneath the pavilion gazing up at the Tathāgata, who by the Buddha’s supernatural power was suspended in mid-air. He then addressed the World-Honored One in verse:
“The World-Honored One abides in great wisdom, Dwelling securely as the Unsurpassed One;
Out of compassion for all sentient beings, I pray that you will accept these lotus flowers.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied to the youth in verse:
“I abide in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), which is not the domain of the world;
that limit has no limit—this is the characteristic of the limit of reality.
At that time, the youth Sucintita asked in verse:
"How does one abide at the limit, O Guide within the ultimate reality?
That limit has no limit; if it does not exist, how can one abide?"
At that time, the World-Honored One answered in verse:
“If the limit is the ultimate reality (bhūtakoṭi), then that very limit is the Tathāgata.
Just as one abides in the ultimate reality, the Guide abides in this same way.”
If the limit is the true limit, then that very limit is the Tathāgata;
as he dwells in the true limit, so do I dwell, O youth!
At that time, the youth Sucintita asked in verse:
"The limitlessness of limits is itself a limit; what are the characteristics of that limit?
By what skillful means is it called the 'limit of reality' (bhūtakoṭi)?"
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
“Without grasping at limits or non-limits, Therefore it is called the ‘Limit of Reality’ (bhūtakoṭi).
Space is the characteristic of this limit; Yet that space has no characteristic of space.”
At that time, the youth Sucintita spoke these verses:
“The sublime state is the true state; Among all places, there is none superior.
May all sentient beings Abide in this, just like the Teacher.”
At that time, the youth Sucintita addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Out of compassion for me, I pray that the World-Honored One will accept these lotus flowers.”
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted the lotus flowers offered by him.
Having accepted them, the Tathāgata spoke these words: "World-Honored One! [the youth said].
By these roots of goodness, may I attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and, for the sake of all sentient beings, analyze and explain that there is no dharma of ordinary persons and no dharma of śrāvakas.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra, amidst the great assembly, addressed the youth Sucintita, saying:
"What dharma have you realized that you preach for the sake of sentient beings?"
At that time, the youth Sucintita replied in verse:
“The Buddhas and their śrāvakas— none among them have attained anything.
I have awakened to such a Dharma, and I shall preach it for the sake of all sentient beings.”
That Dharma is non-existent in the world, and it is likewise beyond verbal expression;
the wise should know that the nature of phenomena is thus.
The Tathāgatas of the past, the unsurpassed Honored Ones among gods and humans—
There is no one who attains this Dharma; the Teacher has entered parinirvāṇa.
In that place there is no realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), nor is there a realm of sentient beings (sattvadhātu).
This is the unsurpassed limit; it is not the domain of the world.
“The Dharma-realm is merely a name; it is through names that one makes distinctions.
There is no distinction in what is distinguished, for such distinction is ultimately non-existent.
At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra addressed the youth Sucintita in verse, saying:
"How does a youth train in this Dharma?
It is a profound and difficult-to-know realm, wherein even the wise are perplexed.
You have been born but a short time ago, yet your wisdom is profoundly penetrating."
In discourse with the śrāvakas, his wisdom is unimpeded;
in every place, he is skillful, clear, and pure— like refined pure gold,
like a king amidst the great assembly, like the moon in the sky.
At that time, the youth Sucintita replied to the Venerable Pūrṇa in verse:
"You now know what you have asked; in that place, there is no arising."
All phenomena have never arisen; who is there to undergo arising?
Not a single phenomenon arises, for its intrinsic nature cannot be found.
This is the nature of all phenomena: when seeking them, they cannot be found.
Both phenomena and the nature of phenomena are unattainable;
both have never existed, yet the Buddha has preached the wondrous Dharma.
This is the first turning, that which was spoken in the Deer Park.
Like grasping at emptiness with a closed fist, he awakens all the śrāvakas.
The sound of the Dharma pervades all things; saving all sentient beings, he expounds them according to reality through the attainment of skillful wisdom.
Birth and death are the realm of ordinary people; Pūrṇa, you still possess them,
for your inversions have not been entirely eliminated.
"Those who are born and those who die—these are the conventional expressions of this world.
Within the Dharma that is beyond expression, such expressions are but secret words.
At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is rare, World-Honored One!
The youth Sudhīmat has attained penetrating wisdom regarding this most profound Dharma.
The Buddha told Pūrṇa:
"It is so, it is so, just as you have said.
The Buddha asked the youth Sucintita:
"For what purpose do you seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"
At that time, the youth Sucintita spoke these verses:
"The Unsurpassed Honored One among gods and humans, Having already known [the answer], you ask nonetheless.
According to what the Muni has taught, Who would have anything to seek?"
I now seek nothing at all, but seek the unimpeded Dharma,
the most profound and unsurpassed word, pure and free from all outflows.
Sentient beings cannot be apprehended, and that which is not a sentient being is likewise so.
Without being deluded or submerged herein, one is able to dwell within the world.
If one can thus understand this profound and unsurpassed statement—
that things are neither identical nor different— it is as explained above regarding the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Awakening all sentient beings, yet sentient beings cannot be apprehended;
because there are no sentient beings, there is likewise no one who awakens.
Wisdom and sentient beings—neither have an intrinsic nature that can be apprehended.
If one can know in this way, they are called a wise person.
World-Honored One!
Being thus, I have spontaneously awakened to this knowledge, and for the sake of all sentient beings, I shall preach the unsurpassed Dharma.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is rare, World-Honored One!

That the youth Sucintita, by means of such profound eloquence, is able to expound upon this dharma of non-realization and non-attainment, causing all the worlds—gods, humans, and asuras—to give rise to awe and trepidation.”
"Bhagavān! Who would not practice and study this Dharma?
One should first practice and study this profound Dharma."
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda spoke these verses:
“The youth Sudarśana, standing amidst the great assembly, Is like the precious mountain Sumeru; all who behold him are filled with joy.”
Just as Mount Sumeru Is securely situated within the great ocean,
So too is this well-spoken Dharma Beloved and cherished by the world.
Neither "existent" nor "non-existent"— Such are the words spoken by the youth.
The reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) as it has been taught is not the domain of the world.
When such words are spoken, do not give rise to a mind of alarm or fear. Tell me now: how is it known to be thus?
At that time, the youth spoke in verse:
“I disregard my own body and life, Seeking the Dharma without attachment;
Thus I seek awakening— O you of great learning, you should know this.”
Because of desire, one falls into confusion and turmoil, and undergoes all manner of sufferings in the world;
I have no longer any greedy attachment, for I have seen the Teacher of the World.
This is the realm of the Buddhas, those who rescue and protect the world.
Now standing before the Buddha, my body is free from all faults.
Both space and my own body are equally ungraspable;
if no dharma can be apprehended, what fear could there be regarding dharmas?
Space and the Buddha—both are unobtainable;
if one can thus endure this, one will have no fear regarding phenomena.
Space and the earth—their intrinsic nature is unobtainable.
Well-reflect upon this intrinsic nature, and you will have no fear regarding phenomena.
Well-reflect upon the ground of space: it was originally non-existent and shall likewise remain so;
being without intrinsic nature and without arising, that which fears has no intrinsic nature.
"Space has no high or low; ultimately it cannot be apprehended.
One who knows phenomena in this way has no fear regarding phenomena.
At that time, the World-Honored One asked the youth Sucintita:
“Are you not afraid? “No, World-Honored One.”
“Are you not startled? “No, World-Honored One.”
The Buddha said to the youth:
"Excellent, excellent!
That you are able to be neither startled nor terrified by this most profound Dharma."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“If one feels fear toward the body, yet finds that this body cannot be apprehended,
and if one practices such constant patience, that person seeks awakening.”
It is said that there is the notion of "sentient beings," yet sentient beings cannot be apprehended;
if one can understand it thus, one dwells securely in this vehicle.
If neither enlightenment nor non-enlightenment is apprehended, [one dwells in this vehicle].
There is nothing further to be attained; thus, one has nothing to fear.
If one can understand it in this way, abiding neither in existence nor non-existence, you should know that this path is bodhi.

"Therefore, Sudānta! A bodhisattva who wishes to swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and wishes to awaken to it, should constantly cultivate the perception of permanence, the perception of bliss, the perception of purity, the perception of a sentient being, and the perception of a person; they should train in this path, which can lead them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."

When I was originally practicing the bodhisattva path, I also constantly cultivated and studied such practices; yet, having attained this unsurpassed path, I did not obtain a single dharma that could be called "attaining bodhi."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"I speak of the notion of permanence, yet the essence of permanence cannot be found.
Since both permanence and impermanence do not exist, it cannot be found even when sought."
Those who perceive sentient beings through the notion of pleasure do not understand that this perception of pleasure is a perverted notion;
it arises from conceptual discrimination regarding persons.
Therefore, they maintain the notions of a "self" and a "person."
If there is one who knows the Dharma, neither "this" nor "that" can be apprehended.
Enlightenment is not attained through a path, nor is it attained apart from a path;
such is the nature of all phenomena—that the Dharma cannot be found when sought.
When it comes to the ultimate reality, the wise do not engage in conceptual discrimination;
you should understand it thus: this path is bodhi.
One who does not practice this wondrous vehicle—the Buddha-vehicle, the unsurpassed vehicle—[does not attain it].
Those who give rise to such conceptual discrimination do not understand the Dharma;
they do not practice this wondrous vehicle—the Buddha-vehicle, the Unsurpassed Vehicle.
If one does not cultivate this practice, the profound samādhi will be difficult to realize.
All phenomena lack substantial reality; substantial reality cannot be found.
If there is no substantial reality, how could there be pleasure?
Whether pleasure or pain, they are like tracks in the sky.
The wise know according to how it is taught, and their minds attain liberation.
When I speak of one who "has a self," that phenomenon lacks any substantial reality; because there is no self, there is no one who knows.
Because there is no knower, this is the sphere of wisdom;
therefore, it is said that the notion of a "life-principle" (jīva-saṃjñā) is ultimately unfindable.
Whether it be a self (ātman) or a life-principle, their intrinsic nature (svabhāva) lacks any substantial reality.
Those of great wisdom can understand and know; those of little wisdom are deluded.
Regarding their nature and actual reality—this is the realm of ordinary beings—who do not know this vehicle, the inconceivable Buddha-vehicle.
The profound sūtras have not been heard nor upheld;
within this dharma-gate, there is no dharma to be expounded.
I have not attained a single dharma, nor is there any dharma to be spoken.
When I sat at the site of enlightenment, I did not realize even a single wisdom.
It is the same with non-wisdom; because there is nothing to be attained in bodhi, both bodhi and the site of enlightenment cannot be apprehended when spoken of.
Ordinary beings give rise to conceptual discrimination, saying, "The Buddha preaches the Dharma.
These are the subtle and secret words, the profound teachings spoken by the Buddha.
If one does not hear this Dharma, which was spoken by the Most Victorious One, [one will not realize it].
The profound and the Buddha—these are the realm of Māra.
Those people do not know its flavor; yet the assembly of all Bodhisattvas, who guard all dharmas, has nothing they do not understand of this Dharma.
The Buddhas and awakening—both are unobtainable.
Such false speech is called "the Buddha preaching the Dharma.
How could such a thing exist? Upon what could it depend for its seeking?
If there are those with wisdom who discern the profoundly deep Dharma,
they will thus believe in and praise the inconceivable Buddhas. Therefore, O Subhūti!
One should study the profound Dharma; its meaning is exceedingly deep, and only those with profound wisdom can awaken to it.
Though it is described in such words, even these words cannot be grasped.
Sentient beings perceive through inversion; this is not their domain.
It is not by means of samādhi alone that one can know this meaning;
both samādhi and non-samādhi do not exist even within emptiness.
This is not the domain of wisdom, nor is it the domain of non-wisdom.
One should realize that this limit is not within the sphere of ordinary wisdom.
When I formerly heard this Dharma and practiced in its most profound depths,
the inclinations of sentient beings differed, and those who could receive it with faith were rare indeed.
"If one does not believe this sutra, which was spoken by the Most Victorious One,
only those who have planted roots of goodness under many Buddhas will be able to believe it.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Suvicintin, saying:
“O youth! Therefore, a bodhisattva should thus adorn himself so as not to give rise to fear in the face of what is terrifying in the world; he should adorn himself in this manner.”
The youth said, “World-Honored One!
I now believe with joy and accept its practice; it is something that foolish people cannot believe.”
The Buddha told the youth:
"I shall explain to you the profound practice of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
All phenomena are without contention; having heard this, one is not startled."
Hearing that all phenomena are severed, one is not startled;
hearing that all phenomena are not severed, one is not startled;
hearing that all phenomena exist or that all phenomena do not exist, one is not startled.
Having heard that all phenomena are conceptual and all phenomena are non-conceptual, they are not startled;
having heard that all phenomena are conditioned and all phenomena are unconditioned, they are not startled;
having heard that all phenomena have objective spheres and all phenomena have no objective spheres, they are not startled.
Hearing that all phenomena are joyful and all phenomena are without joy, one is not startled;
hearing that all phenomena are differentiated and all phenomena are without differentiation, one is not startled;
hearing that all phenomena involve seeking and all phenomena involve no seeking, one is not startled.
All phenomena are cool, yet all phenomena are not cool; having heard this, one is not startled.
All phenomena are luminous, yet all phenomena are not luminous; having heard this, one is not startled.
All phenomena have names, yet all phenomena are nameless; having heard this, one is not startled.
Having heard that all phenomena arise and all phenomena are unarisen, one is not startled;
having heard that all phenomena have fear and all phenomena are fearless, one is not startled;
having heard that all phenomena arise, all phenomena cease, and all phenomena are unceasing, one is not startled.
Hearing that "all phenomena are the path" and "all phenomena are not the path," one is not startled;
hearing that "all phenomena are parinirvāṇa" and "all phenomena are not parinirvāṇa," one is not startled.
"When this Dharma is taught, no fear or alarm arises.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"In all phenomena, Their intrinsic nature cannot be found."
Because they lack intrinsic nature, one should contemplate the cessation of their marks.
All phenomena are without cessation, and within them there is no mind;
because all phenomena do not exist, their intrinsic nature cannot be apprehended.
In all phenomena there is contention, yet their mind cannot be apprehended;
if phenomena cannot be apprehended, there is likewise no one who contends.
Because all phenomena do not exist, their nature has no reality.
If intrinsic nature were non-existent, then phenomena would likewise not cease.
When all phenomena are severed, the wise understand them as non-dual;
this is called "severance," yet it does not manifest as a state of cessation.
All phenomena are uninterrupted; even a single atom cannot be found.
Whether as a single atom or a multitude of atoms, they cannot be found within phenomena.
Because all phenomena are non-existent, they appear within the realm of verbal expression.
Just as that [self] cannot be found, though it truly exists yet does not appear;
because all phenomena are non-existent, they are seen through skillful means.
To claim that they lack reality is merely conceptual proliferation.
All phenomena are in harmony; they are taught as being without contention.
When one seeks the intrinsic nature of contention, it is ultimately found to have no reality.
All phenomena are without conjunction; they are neither created nor extinguished.
Thus it is unattainable, being far removed from all phenomena.
All phenomena are unobtainable; their beginning cannot be found because they have no beginning.
Therefore, this is called the "Reality Limit" (bhūtakoṭi).
All phenomena are joyful, yet this joy is unattainable;
if phenomena are unattainable, they are also beyond verbal expression.
All phenomena are without joy, for phenomena are non-dual.
In the intrinsic nature there is no reality; this is the mark of profundity.
The single-natured dharma is immovable, and within the intrinsic nature there is no self.
Because the intrinsic nature does not exist, movement cannot be found when sought.
Immovability is nirvāṇa; the Dharma cannot be found, for no dharma exists—therefore it is called nirvāṇa.
All dharmas are impermanent, yet the ultimate truth is taught.
These verbal expressions of sentient beings are called "conceptualization.
All phenomena are without conceptualization, for they are impermanent and lack abiding.
Sentient beings cannot be apprehended; this is the Dharma within the Dharma.
All phenomena are like illusions, yet those illusions cannot be apprehended;
because phenomena cannot be apprehended, they are spoken of based on conventional practice.
All phenomena are unconditioned; this is their very nature.
Because dharmas cannot be apprehended, they are therefore called "boundless.
Regarding the realm that is spoken of, its own essence is devoid of a realm;
yet ordinary beings grasp at it through delusion and declare, "There is a realm."
The Sovereign speaks of objective spheres, yet also speaks of the absence of objective spheres;
because he speaks of objective spheres, one should know that there is no objective sphere.
All phenomena are real, yet their number cannot be apprehended.
If the body cannot be apprehended, therefore there is no difference between them.
Because there is nothing to be apprehended, one knows that there is something apprehended;
because there is something apprehended, one knows that there is nothing apprehended.
Within it there is no coolness, nor is there anything that is not cool;
there is no dharma and no coolness—this is the reality of all dharmas.
All dharmas are unattainable, and this cannot be expressed in words.
Because all phenomena are non-existent, one knows that all phenomena exist.
All phenomena are merely names, yet even names cannot be apprehended.
If phenomena cannot be apprehended, then one knows there is nirvāṇa.
Feeling and non-feeling are spoken of within feeling;
herein there is nothing to be spoken of, yet it is designated as "speaking.
That which is called "existence" is not existence; it is spoken of within existence.
Because they give rise to conceptual discrimination, they constantly fall into the extremes of existence and non-existence.
When ordinary people see an illusory person, they grasp at it and claim it to be real;
yet the equality of existence and non-existence does not confuse the wise when they hear of it.
The arising of phenomena and their non-arising—both are unattainable.
It is for the sake of inferior ordinary beings that one speaks of the arising of phenomena.
If phenomena were to have an arising, they would necessarily have a cessation.
The phenomenon of arising and the phenomenon of ceasing—these two are unattainable.
All phenomena are entirely empty; no phenomenon can be apprehended.
You should understand this as the profound Dharma that I have taught.
Awakening is beyond verbal expression, and there is no agent who creates it;
when awakening is attained, one clearly understands the three realms of existence.
If one discriminates awakening, that is not called seeking awakening.
Practice and enlightenment possess no marks of conceptual differentiation.
All phenomena are unarisen; even when seeking their intrinsic nature, it is not found.
Because intrinsic nature does not exist, this is the characteristic of nirvāṇa.
Ultimately there is no arising; it cannot be found when sought, because its intrinsic nature does not exist. It is neither extinguished nor non-extinguished.
One who understands this meaning [realizes] the intrinsic nature of all phenomena.
Because they have no birth, they are free from conflict and strife.
Those who hear the teaching of the profound Dharma and do not give rise to alarm or fear—
know that such beings, the Buddha declares, are bodhisattvas.
At that time, the youth Sucintita addressed the Buddha in verse:
“The World-Honored One, the Unsurpassed Teacher, has appeared in the world for my sake;
within this Dharma, he teaches that one seeks only names through diverse characteristics.”
The Muni has appeared in the world; the Buddha’s birth is inconceivable.
Having forever severed the nets of all Māras, he manifests the net of the True Dharma.
I have severed birth and death completely; before long, I shall reach the site of enlightenment.
If there were no conceptualization of difference, one would teach by means of signs.
The World-Honored One has taught what is to be sought; having seen it, one enters nirvāṇa, delivers the entire world, and cuts off all doubts.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the youth Sucintita, saying:
"The practice free from doubt and hesitation is the bodhisattva practice;
the practice of protective mindfulness is the bodhisattva practice."
Non-conceptual practice, free from all faults, which out of profound conduct compassionates all sentient beings equally—this is the practice of a bodhisattva.
Well-considered!

The practice of signs and the practice of falsehood are the characteristics of desire; by abandoning the practice of desire, one becomes free from all anger and resentment, maintaining a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings because the mind cannot be apprehended;
one practices great loving-kindness for the sake of seeking the Dharma;
and one practices great giving because of non-abandonment.
He practices conduct free from doubt, because he perceives no other;
he practices conduct free from affliction and fever, because it is cool and refreshing;
he practices conduct of diligence, because he is without weariness.
They practice the conduct of samādhi, because their minds are boundless;
they practice the conduct of wisdom, because they know the characteristics of all phenomena;
they practice the conduct of fearlessness, because they are free from timidity.
They practice unobstructed conduct, because they accomplish the supreme conduct that manifests the image of the Tathāgata;
they observe all worlds in the ten directions, because their conduct is unhindered.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"I explain the practices of all bodhisattvas, Which are far removed from all doubt and confusion;
Both [doubt] and ignorance Are ultimately unobtainable."
To practice that which is not practice—this is the practice of all bodhisattvas.
If one knows this practice, then that person's practice is unimpeded.
To speak of all bodhisattvas alike, they maintain mindful protection over all dharmas.
Seeking through non-attainment—this is the supreme practice.
If one says, "I am practicing," one dwells in perversion;
because of dwelling in perversion, one cannot attain fearlessness.
This is the practice of verbal expression, yet verbal expression cannot be apprehended;
if one can understand it thus, one practices the Unsurpassed Vehicle.
This Great Vehicle, this Unsurpassed Vehicle—this vehicle is free from alarm and fear.
Fear and fearlessness—both are conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*).
I teach that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are non-existent;
if all conditioned phenomena are non-existent, this is the supreme practice.
This practice is profound, guarding and mindful of all phenomena;
both this guarding and mindfulness, as well as this profundity, are entirely conceptual constructions.
Within this, both the profound and the practice are utterly non-existent.
If one knows this limit, one does not differentiate among phenomena.
There is no phenomenon to be grasped or attached to, nor is there any phenomenon that cannot be so;
this is the nature of all phenomena, which is taught as being devoid of intrinsic nature.
There is no solidity, no desire, and so forth; these are taught for the sake of seeking.
Since syllables cannot be apprehended, this is the unsurpassed phrase.
I have spoken this through skillful means; let those who hear it not give rise to fear.
Seeking them, they cannot be found, nor do they possess any characteristic of destruction.
These activities of all sentient beings are in truth unfindable;
if one can know them thus, this is called skillful cultivation and study.
All sentient beings do not exist; therefore, I speak of "sentient beings.
Yet the nature of sentient beings is such that this path is unsurpassed.
Whether it be mind or sentient beings, ultimately they cannot be apprehended.
This is the primary meaning, spoken out of great compassion.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, a great donor of the world,
is called a "donor" because he practices constant giving.
If phenomena cannot be apprehended, and all phenomena are thus non-existent, then at that time,
the one who practices giving does so because the bodhisattva lacks [discriminative] wisdom.
If phenomena cannot be apprehended, then amidst phenomena of high and low, [there is no distinction].
Because they are free from fear and dread, they are called true donors.
If the Buddha cannot be apprehended, then the Dharma is inconceivable;
this is called true upholding of the precepts, wherein all phenomena have no basis.
The Buddha-realm is inconceivable; it is taught for the sake of all bodhisattvas.
The foolish do not awaken to this, and thus their prohibitions and precepts are not pure.
They give rise to patience toward sentient beings, yet sentient beings cannot be apprehended.
This is the unsurpassed patience, which is taught within this Dharma;
if the mind cannot be apprehended, and there is likewise no conceptual discrimination—
this is the unsurpassed patience, because phenomena cannot be apprehended.
When weariness arises, the bodhisattva should distance themselves from such superior diligence, which is spoken of merely by name; rather,
they should practice the straight diligence of body and mind, remaining non-reliant upon all phenomena.
This is the supreme diligence taught for all bodhisattvas.
When a bodhisattva, amidst the teachings, does not give rise to weariness, their diligence is effortless; such diligent application is unsurpassed.
Within all internal and external phenomena, the nature of the mind cannot be apprehended;
for the mind is well-tamed and supple because the mind is unapprehendable.
Both the objects of perception and the mind itself have no inherent self-nature.
The samādhi of no-mind is therefore called samāpatti.
O Sugata, explain this to me: if one does not depart from this dharma, I say that one is well-tamed.
One does not know through wisdom that phenomena possess even the slightest intrinsic nature;
both intrinsic nature and phenomena—these two are ultimately non-existent.
One cannot apprehend any phenomenon within the sphere of the mind and consciousness.
One does not know phenomena through cognition, for their intrinsic nature is ultimately non-existent.
If one can understand in this way, this is the power of mindfulness of a bodhisattva;
they practice the ultimate truth, which is not the domain of the mundane world.
All beings are without reality, yet for them one preaches the True Teaching;
amidst that great assembly, one does not give rise to the notion of "sentient beings.
Those beings are like illusions, and those illusions are ultimately non-existent.
When hearing such teachings, one does not give rise to the notion of obstruction.
If both self and other dharmas— these two— are ultimately non-existent,
then upon hearing such teachings, one does not give rise to the notion of obstruction.
The two dharmas of internal and external are practiced by the wise;
because their minds have no sense of high or low, all worlds are equal.
All phenomena are unimpeded, like tracks left in the sky.
The intrinsic nature of phenomena is likewise, like a track in the sky.
When a bodhisattva knows this, they are said to have attained thorough mastery;
clearly understanding all phenomena, they know the conduct of sentient beings.
Sentient beings cannot be apprehended, and the seeking of the Dharma is likewise so;
with wisdom one clearly understands all realms, yet those realms are ultimately non-existent.
I say that by entering this gate, one practices the unsurpassed path.
Having attained such a path, one knows the conduct of all sentient beings.
Both the elements (*dhātu*) and sentient beings—these two are both devoid of reality.
Such is the foremost wisdom that knows all phenomena.
Regarding internal and external phenomena, wisdom is without attachment;
being far removed from the dharma of non-attachment, this is called the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
This dharma is inconceivable and is named the Buddha-dharma of all Buddhas.
Those phenomena have no existence; even non-existence is ultimately non-existent.
When practicing in this way, one does not cling to this world.
This wisdom is called "unimpeded," and it is known as the wisdom of all Buddhas.
All phenomena are inconceivable; in the principle of dharmas, there is no reality.
Because these dharmas do not exist, the Buddha-dharma is called "Awakening.
Regarding all Buddhas and the Buddha-dharma, one remains entirely unattached.
Not clinging to awakening—this is called the wisdom of all Buddhas.
This vehicle is the Great Vehicle; it encompasses all dharma-gates, delivering and liberating all worlds, yet no world can be apprehended.
In all worlds, toward all sentient beings,
the Bodhisattva, seeking the Dharma, approaches them with intimacy and reverence.
Deeply contemplating these phenomena, he realizes that the Buddha-Dharma is inconceivable.
Because they do not apprehend any phenomena, these people attain bodhi.
Both bodhi and all phenomena are entirely without marks;
those who observe in this way can exhaustively realize the Buddha-dharma.
When observing in this manner, one does not cling to the world;
because the mind does not cling, one is able to bring enlightenment to its consummation. "Furthermore, Sudhyāyin!"
I shall now speak concerning those Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who have not yet perfected their adornments.

If there are those who, upon hearing such a Dharma-gate as this, do not give rise to fear or alarm, you should know that these persons are already near the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and close to the realm of the Buddhas. Abiding in the path of unobstructed liberation, they observe the ten directions with minds free from attachment; they are thus protected and sustained by all Buddhas through great loving-kindness, great compassion, the unique Buddha-dharmas, and the invisible crown-mark.
Those who, upon hearing such a profound Dharma-gate, give rise to faith and joy, are all seen and known by the Tathāgata;
those who do not have faith or joy in this sutra, the Tathāgata also knows them all.
"Those who give rise to faith and joy in this sutra are the disciples of the Buddha; I am their teacher.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"I have already sat at the site of enlightenment, And the site of enlightenment is ultimately empty."
Because enlightenment cannot be attained, one dwells securely within wisdom.
That Dharma is without obstruction; the essence of phenomena is ultimately non-existent.
If phenomena are ultimately non-existent, this is known at the time of liberation.
Among all phenomena, wisdom can reach the Buddha;
that all phenomena and wisdom are thus—this is what the Buddha has taught.
Ordinary beings engage in false conceptualization, speaking of existence and non-existence with attachment.
The Buddhas do not make distinctions, nor do the Bodhisattvas or the wise.
When they observe all worlds, they see that the world is ultimately non-existent;
because the world is empty and quiescent, the wisdom that observes it is likewise so.
Sentient beings and Buddhas possess no marks of distinction;
because they are without such distinctions, it is called supreme compassion.
Even though one is touched by pity throughout the entire realm of sentient beings, [it remains free from conceptualization].
That compassion has no substantial reality, yet compassion extends to that which possesses substantial reality.
This is the realm of ordinary beings; it is like measuring the dimensions of space—originally non-existent and never to be found—and the world is likewise so.
This is called supreme compassion; this is the unsurpassed Dharma, known as the Dharma of all Buddhas, which cannot be found even when sought.
Thus spoke the Sugata, the Teacher, the Unsurpassed Honored One.
Form cannot be found when sought; likewise, phenomena are formless.
It is spoken of in accordance with worldly convention that space is without limit and cannot be grasped anywhere; such is the nature of all Buddha-dharmas.
It is spoken of in accordance with the world;
this unsurpassed wisdom cannot be apprehended, because wisdom itself is unapprehendable.
That wisdom is likewise without reality, whether it be this shore or the further shore.
It is spoken of by way of characteristics;
because they grasp at characteristics, they do not practice the profound Dharma.
All things are equal; if one were to speak of them by way of characteristics, [it would be a mistake].
Then they are not spiritual friends.
If they say that there is something to be sought, because they speak by grasping at signs,
they are not spiritual friends.
If one were to say that phenomena exist, and that by eliminating them one attains non-existence—O Youth!
regarding this Dharma of mine, I do not speak in such a way.
Within the intrinsic nature there is no suffering; if one were to speak thus, [it would be a misconception].
Not entering into this Dharma is what is called "accumulation" (saṃudaya); if one speaks of abandoning accumulation,
then one is far removed from this Dharma.
To discriminate that which is fundamentally non-existent— within the dharma of fundamental non-existence,
there has never been any cessation.
If one speaks through discrimination, how could that which was fundamentally non-existent now cease?
"O youth! You should know that this view is not the right view.
Those who cultivate the Path speak thus for the sake of seeking."
I entrust this to those who seek it, so that they may practice and study upon the Path.
Those of great wisdom and great renown will, in future ages,
be able to understand this profound meaning.
The Supreme One has taught these various roots of goodness for the sake of all sentient beings.
The wise are able to receive and uphold them; such persons, in future lives, will—
They are able to protect my True Dharma,
abiding in suchness free from conceptual discrimination; this is bodhi,
yet bodhi is unattainable.

When this Dharma was being taught, the youth Sucintita attained the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), leaping for joy and experiencing what he had never known before.
It is the constant practice of all Buddhas that when they bestow a prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa) upon bodhisattvas, they manifest such rare and wondrous events.
At that time, the World-Honored One emitted various rays of light from his face—blue, yellow, red, white, purple, and crystal-colored.

Once these lights had issued forth, they illuminated all the immeasurable worlds above, reaching as far as the Brahma realm. Having illuminated the worlds, they returned to the presence of the Buddha, circled him three times, and entered through the crown of his head.
At that time, the great earth shook in six ways.
Then, there were hosts of devas in the air who rained down various celestial flowers, aloeswood, and powdered incense, while performing celestial music in the void and producing wondrous sounds.
At that time, the trichiliocosm was pure and adorned like Uttarakuru.
Then Ānanda rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"For what cause and condition does the Tathāgata manifest this rare event?
If there were no cause and condition, the Tathāgata would not manifest such an auspicious sign.
At that time, Ānanda spoke in verse:
“O Unsurpassed Guide, Honored One among Men, Without a cause, you do not manifest such wondrous transformations.
I pray that the World-Honored One will explain for the sake of the assembly: What is the cause and condition for these auspicious signs now?”
The devas dwelling in the midst of the void Make offerings to the Most Victorious, Unsurpassed Honored One;
With joyful leaps they offer praise, As he skillfully expounds the subtle and supreme Dharma-gate.
Just as the northern continent of Uttarakuru is adorned with various kinds of exquisite flowers, so too are these rays of light;
they illuminate this world, making it entirely pure and magnificent.

The Dharma of all Buddhas is thus: they bestow predictions upon the bodhisattvas, emitting this great light of wondrous color that shines everywhere throughout the ten directions and enters through the crown of the head.
O Unsurpassed One of Supreme Diligence, the Honored Muni, you manifest this rare event of radiant light;
for what reason does the Tathāgata emit this light?
I pray that, out of great compassion, you will explain it to me.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses for Ānanda:
“The youth Suvicintita, Having extensively planted all roots of goodness In the presence of the Tathāgatas, Shall become the Honored One among men.”
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"This youth Subhāṣita shall, in a future age, come to make offerings to countless billions of Buddhas. In the presence of those Buddhas, he will have faith, joy, and reverence, and shall provide them with all manner of requisites—food and drink, clothing, bedding, and medicinal elixirs—to make offerings to those Buddhas."

After those Tathāgatas have entered parinirvāṇa, one shall take their Buddha-relics and erect great jeweled stupas a hundred thousand yojanas high, adorned with every kind of precious gem, and honor, praise, and make offerings to those Tathāgatas with all manner of flowers, incense, jeweled banners, pennants, canopies, sandalwood, aloeswood, various powdered incenses, music, songs, and hymns.

When you attain Buddhahood, you shall be known as the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, named Viśuddhacandra.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“In all the worlds of the ten directions, If they were filled with precious jewels,
And one were to offer this heap of treasures To all the Tathāgatas.”
"The World-Honored One has taught that if one hears and is able to uphold the teachings of the Unsurpassed Teacher of the world, the merit thereof shall be greater than that.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha in verse:
"This profound and supreme Dharma-gate, spoken by the Most Victorious One—
what is the name of this sutra?
We shall receive and uphold it upon our heads."
Within this Dharma-gate, it is not said that even a single dharma is non-existent, nor can existence be apprehended; such is what is taught in the supreme Dharma-gate.
All contaminated dharmas, as well as uncontaminated dharmas—
In this, nothing can be apprehended, as taught in the subtle and wondrous sūtra.
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) and the unconditioned realm (*asaṃskṛta-dhātu*)—both are unapprehendable; this is what is taught within this sūtra.
The World-Honored One, the Unsurpassed Teacher, has taught that all conditioned phenomena are entirely ungraspable; this is what is proclaimed in this sutra.
That which the Buddha has taught is not even spoken of here.
What has been taught is most subtle; though one seeks me, I cannot be found.
Throughout all the worlds of the ten directions, that which the World-Honored One has taught is that these worlds possess no intrinsic nature; this is what is explained within this sutra.
O Unsurpassed Honored Teacher, we pray that you will tell us:
what is the name of this sutra?
We shall receive and uphold it.
Having heard these words, the Buddha told Śāriputra:
“This sūtra is named ‘The Crown King. Its crown is ultimately non-existent;
you of great wisdom should know this and uphold it accordingly.”
If one can receive and uphold this, which was spoken by the Most Victorious One,
that person will be able to awaken to the knowledge of all devas and worldly beings.
When the Buddha spoke this Dharma, there were hundreds of thousands of people in the assembly.
All their roots of goodness increase, and they all resolve upon bodhicitta.
"Because they have heard this sutra, this most profound and unsurpassed Dharma,
this assembly shall surely attain the state of the Unsurpassed Honored One in the world."
Within the profound Dharma, they shall all attain complete understanding;
this assembly shall eventually act thus, upholding these verses.
If one can uphold this *Uṣṇīṣarāja Sūtra* as it has been taught, [one shall likewise attain such realization].
Within all phenomena, do not give rise to a mind of expectation.
Herein there is not even a single patience, nor is there a second patience;
if phenomena cannot be apprehended, then there is no dharma that can be spoken of.
If there are those who can receive and uphold the *Uṣṇīṣarāja-sūtra*,
by contemplating this Dharma, they will be able to give rise to eloquence;
if there is a wise woman who can receive and uphold this sutra, [she too shall attain such power].
One can swiftly transform the female body and accomplish the qualities of a man.
Knowing one thing is to know all; by means of this knowledge of all, the dhāraṇī of all phenomena is expounded within this sūtra.
All phenomena are expressed through speech, and they encompass all things;
thus this section is explained, such that the light of the Dharma pervades everywhere.
One should know the various names applied to each of those worlds.
That which is taught in various places—its dharma cannot be apprehended.
Since dharma cannot be taken as an object of perception, it cannot be found even when sought;
all dharmas are thus, and the one who possesses the dhāraṇī dwells in peace and happiness.
If phenomena are ungraspable, and within phenomena there is neither existence nor non-existence—
this is the nature of all phenomena, which is called the dhāraṇī.
If there is one who can uphold this King of Pinnacles Sūtra as it has been taught, [they shall attain liberation].
The radiance of upholding the Dharma Shines universally upon all places.
All phenomena are profoundly deep; That Dharma cannot be apprehended.
If a phenomenon cannot be apprehended, It is neither existent nor non-existent.
If a person possesses wisdom and eloquence that is unimpeded, they will be able to know this meaning: that ultimately nothing has any substantial reality.
It is like the dragon of Anavatapta, who dwells in the sky and pours down great rain.
Water does not come from without; it is thus through the power of the inconceivable.
If one wishes to know all phenomena, one should discern them without obstruction;
by studying this sutra, one does not rely on any phenomena.
Within this Dharma-gate, phenomena come from nowhere;
all phenomena are unarisen—this is what is taught in this sutra.
It is like the light of the sun: there is no place its radiance does not reach.
This sutra is likewise, illuminating all phenomena.
If there is a bhikṣu of eloquence, he should receive and uphold this sutra;
he should study this Sūtra, the Subtle and Wondrous King of Summits.
One will swiftly attain inconceivable eloquence;
having studied this sutra, one can benefit the world.
If there are those who, regarding this sutra, can believe in it and give rise to sympathetic joy,
The dhāraṇī is difficult to obtain, for its flavor is not known.
If bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs do not practice this,
but instead engage in other vain practices, they are very far from my Dharma.
Among my disciples, those who are able to practice this can become the eye of the world; none can equal them.
Like the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, they are able to protect and shelter the world.
This sutra is also like this, able to serve as a shelter for the world.
Just as one standing on the peak of Mount Sumeru sees all the world;
so too, dwelling in this sutra, one observes all phenomena.
Just as a falling meteor is seen by all at night,
The radiance of one who upholds this sutra is supreme among all dharmas.
It is like the light of the sun, Which shines everywhere throughout all places.
This sutra is also like this, capable of extinguishing all darkness.
Like the moon in the sky, which shines and does not remain;
this sutra is also like this, capable of illuminating the worlds of the ten directions.
This seal is the Dharma-seal, the seal upon which all seals are impressed;
this seal abides in the world for the sake of all bodhisattvas.
Like a seal in the void, it was originally non-existent and shall likewise never exist.
Space and the seal—both are conceptual constructions.
Thus are all Buddha-dharmas explained in this sutra:
the Buddhas are ineffable, and the dharmas are likewise so.
Just as when a king’s life is nearing its end, he entrusts the succession of the state to his eldest son and issues a decree to the assembly of ministers:
"Entrust everything to my son."
Such is the wealth of the noble Dharma, protected by the worthy sages;
it is entrusted to the bhikṣu Ānanda to be expounded for the sake of all bodhisattvas.
To protect and uphold this sutra for the sake of all bodhisattvas—
Those who have perfected their roots of goodness—into their hands this sutra shall enter.
If there are those who can receive and uphold it, and expound upon this sutra, such persons will surely attain Buddhahood; of this there is no doubt.
If a person seeks eloquence and has no dependence on phenomena,
they should receive, uphold, and expound this supreme Dharma-gate of the Crown King.
To speak of worldly dharmas is itself called bodhi.
Thus, without distinction, one who penetrates this sutra will have no doubt regarding any world;
such a person is able to uphold this sutra and also explain it to others.
Having heard this sutra, they realize the teachings of all Buddhas;
by means of this profound Dharma, they bring benefit to all sentient beings.
When the Buddha spoke this sutra, all the Buddhas praised it in unison.
“Excellent, O Unsurpassed Honored One!
What you have spoken is most subtle and wondrous.
You have raised this great banner of the Dharma—a banner of the Dharma that is inconceivable.”
If one can use even a four-line verse to explain it for sentient beings—
this inconceivable sutra— if one explains it for others,
one will be able to contemplate immeasurable dharmas; such contemplation of dharmas is inconceivable.
"The Buddhas, the Unsurpassed Honored Ones, Have forever severed all phenomena;
They all alike preach this sutra, This inconceivable Dharma-gate.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:

"If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who, having heard this Dharma, receive, uphold, recite, and explain it to others, the merit they obtain will be exceedingly great, immeasurable, and inexhaustible."
Just as space cannot be exhausted, so it is, Ānanda!

If a person receives, maintains, recites, or reads even a single four-line verse of this profound Dharma-gate and explains it for others, the merit of that person shall likewise be such that it cannot be fully described.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The boundless and profound Dharma— This sutra expounds its great meaning.
Those who receive, uphold, explain, and interpret it Should well protect this sutra."
Even if one were to attempt to describe it through analytical exposition, the sky might yet be measured to its limit;
but regarding the merit of this sutra, even speaking of it cannot exhaust it.
If one receives and upholds this sutra, it is as if one has already made offerings to [all the Buddhas].
Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, to all the World-Honored Ones;
throughout the worlds of the ten directions, wherever the Great Munis may dwell—
to those who uphold this sutra, one shall pay homage and make offerings.
Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, those Honored Ones who possess the ten titles—
if anyone hears this sutra, they have thereby already made offerings to all the World-Honored Ones of the past as well as the Buddhas of the future.
Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, those who are currently the Honored Ones among men—
if there are any who receive and uphold this sutra spoken by the Tathāgata,
they have all already made offerings to the Lion-like Muni, the Honored One.
To provide material offerings is the wisdom of the world;
but for one who upholds this sutra, it is the offering of unsurpassed wisdom.
Even if one were to fill the worlds of the ten directions with rare jewels,
To take these and offer them to all Buddhas brings forth exceedingly great merit;
yet if one further studies this sutra well and explains it to others,
the Buddha declares that the offerings made to such a person are the foremost.
Within the Dharma I have taught, a Buddha cannot be found;
one who is not startled or terrified by this is truly making offerings to the Buddha.
This is the foremost offering, which surpasses anything in the world.
If one does not disparage [them], this too is called making an offering.
Since neither the Buddhas nor the Dharma can be found when sought,
this is the foremost offering, as taught by the Most Victorious One.
To the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara, I made this offering of the Dharma; this is the foremost offering, as taught for all bodhisattvas.
Having made this offering to that Blessed One, I—
Thereafter, one receives the prediction that in a future age one shall become a Buddha.
If you wish to seek the path of the Buddha and become a leader among sentient beings,
practice this path with purity and make offerings to the Teacher.
Having made such offerings, one will attain enlightenment before long;
one should practice these offerings to penetrate all phenomena.
This is the foremost offering: the Dharma of all Buddhas.
All the World-Honored Ones, the Guides, have fully attained it.
Having entered the Buddha’s realm, with inconceivable Buddha-wisdom, they are able to let out the lion’s roar:
"I am worthy to receive the offerings of the world."
Having let out the lion’s roar, he is fearless regarding all phenomena;
he delivers immeasurable sentient beings and enters the untainted *nirvāṇa*.

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the youth Sucintita, the assembly of bhikṣus, and all those in the world—gods, humans, asuras, gandharvas, and others—hearing what the Buddha had spoken, were all greatly rejoiced, and they faithfully accepted and practiced it.
The Mahāyāna Sūtra of the Crown King (Mahāyāna-śīrṣarāja-sūtra)
